utterances.text: Again, where he was born, how you knew him, that's not the question. Why and how do you know that he commanded these attacks I just mentioned? Were you present during the attacks, did you hear it from someone; and, if so, from whom? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Vinko Bojic we heard that he was in command in these places, Rogatica, Gorazde. We heard about that from Vinko who was the prison warden. That's what he said to us when we came to prison, Vinko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And looking at paragraph 57 of your statement, what is the basis of your knowledge that Razdoljac, Djuko, was issuing orders to commanders of the prisons?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Barracks were right by the prison, and when we were in prison he came to the prison. He always asked Vinko for us to go out and to unload ammunition and other things that came to Rogatica. As for all of this information, we heard about all that from Vinko Bojic. He told us who was who, and that's what I heard from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say that this individual, Djuko, Razdoljac was issuing orders to commanders of the prison, would that include the Rasadnik prison?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rasadnik was the prison and he came there and he told Vinko to give him these prisoners to unload things. He didn't ask. He just said, You will give me such and such a number of people to unload ammunition. And it was mostly ammunition that we unloaded there where he was, at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How do you reconcile that with your statement at paragraph 44 wherein you state that Rajko Kusic had 100 per cent control over Rasadnik prison. Are these the same individuals or different individuals?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already described Rajko Kusic, I think, when he came to the prison. And to be very accurate, there were four or five inmates who worked with Rajko Kusic in the same company, that is Huso Krajina, Vatar Semso, Mujo Jasarevic, Orso [phoen], all of them had worked with Rajko Kusic and knew him very well. Further on, when I was arrested, I was brought before Rajko Kusic and that is how he introduced himself. He said that he was Rajko Kusic. Also, when we were supposed to be exchanged, he came and he said that he would no longer feed us, that he would send us to Alija so that Alija could feed us, and that's already contained in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Two last points, sir. In your proofing session relating to Mr. Mladic, you are quoted as saying that you believe Mladic is a butcher and your opinion is that "everything what happened in the camps was Mladic's idea." Sir this accurately reflect your sentiments?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and yet you never saw Mladic at any of the camps or prisons that you were at, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him in any one of the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are these your personal sentiments or something that someone else told you to say at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, these are my personal feelings. When he said that we should all be christened and that we would be transferred to Alija's state, and there's nothing that I didn't mention in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, at low voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that apart from the encounter that you have testified about, you never once encountered Mladic again, and, thus, never saw him committing any acts -- harming any individual in your presence?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That time I saw him where I was -- well, I never saw him again. Except for that one time that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I want to put it to you - and this is my final question, sir - or ask you: Does your personal sentiment towards Mr. Mladic mean that you are willing to do whatever it takes to get him convicted?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would do whatever I could to have him convicted as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I put one additional question in relation to that. Would you also not tell the truth in order to achieve that Mr. Mladic would be convicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Just what I said. I stand by that. And that offended me terribly. When he said that we either had to be christened or transferred to Alija's state. And there was no other way out for me. I could only be destroyed. That's why I'm offended. And I wouldn't say anything else. I never saw him again. That was the only time that I saw him, and that's what I told you about and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever you would be prepared to do, that would not include giving false testimony; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] False testimony? No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does it mean to be christened or transferred to Alija's state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, christened means to have us converted, to change our religion; that we'd no longer be Muslims, that we'd be Serbs. And if we didn't want to do that, then they would transfer us to that state. And I didn't say that in my statement. If he had a state. That's what he said. So if had a state. So -- I mean, if he doesn't have a state, and if I don't want to convert to Christianity, then I'd be destroyed. And the suffering I experienced in camp. I cannot describe that. You cannot believe that. Twenty-six months, it's the command that ordered them to do all of that. We were stripped naked in camp and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You have told us about that. I just wanted to know what it meant to be taken to Alija's state. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you think you could finish that in the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Couple meaning about three or four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five, six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I may need a little bit more time than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately how much?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would say probably closer to ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, unless there is any urgent reason why we shouldn't do that, I would like Ms. Hochhauser to re-examine the witness in the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, at page 39 of today's transcript at line 20, Mr. Ivetic said -- asked -- said to you you testified in two proceedings in state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina wherein you never mentioned this encounter with Mr. Mladic. Do you recall that question? My -- my question to you is: Did anyone in the state courts or during that proceeding ever ask you about an interaction with Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Similarly, you first informed the Office of the Prosecutor about this interaction after testifying in the Karadzic case. To the best of your recollection, were you specifically asked by anyone about Mr. Mladic in -- when doing any of the other -- the previous statements that you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So -- yes, in preparation for the prior statements that you gave to the OTP, both the amalgamated statement that is in evidence now and the statement that you gave in 1999, were you ever asked a specific question about Mr. Mladic? Were you ever asked whether you had any interaction with him or had anything to say about him?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified here in the Karadzic case, and when the hearing was over, then I said to a Prosecutor that I had seen Karadzic -- no, not him, Mladic. And I wanted to describe it, and he said that it wasn't necessary. So that was last time here. As for Mladic, I talked about him when I just got out of prison, and they took me to some military corps. Now I don't know where that was. And I gave an extensive statement there about everything, and I mentioned Mladic there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: sir, you've just told us about the circumstance after testifying in Karadzic when you first raised -- brought to the Prosecutor's attention the incident with Mr. Mladic. My question to you is prior -- before that conversation, where -- where you were asked if you had seen Karadzic and you said, No, I never saw Karadzic, but I did see Mladic, before that, were you ever asked in preparation for any of the OTP statements that you gave here to the ICTY, were you asked about Mr. Mladic -- were you asked a question about Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've told us -- you were asked a series of questions about the -- about your statement at paragraphs 51 through 60, about how you knew about the -- about people that were on the Rogatica Crisis Staff. So drawing your attention to that series of questions, if I can point you --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could have, please, 164 -- Exhibit 164 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if I could point you to the -- paragraph 55. I believe it should be page 11 in the English. Now, you told us when you were answering that series of questions in regard to, and please forgive me if I mispronounce the name, but it's Razdoljac - is it? - aka Djoko, you told us about him, that he had appeared at Rasadnik and that was some of the basis for your knowledge. Did you have the opportunity at other times to overhear Serb soldiers talking about other members of the Crisis Staff and other people who were involved in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. All these persons you mentioned here, I heard about that from several Serb soldiers. I can't remember now. And that's why I said that they were in the top of that command, Razdoljac was there and he came often to the prison, and he could actually ask for inmates to come out even without Vinko. How many were needed to unload the ammunition. I've said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And in the 20-plus months that you were at Rasadnik, did you have other opportunities to see any of these other people that are listed in those paragraphs 52 through -- through 60, did you have other opportunities to see them at Rasadnik and also to hear conversations amongst them?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity of seeing some of these people have I have enumerated, but it was difficult for me to hear the conversations that they held amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to clarify, does that mean that the persons you commented upon being the members of the Crisis Staff, that they were present in the place where you were detained, that is, in Rasadnik prison? Did you see them there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them or some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw all five of them, but they weren't together on the same day. Sometimes there would be one of them who was present. On other occasions it would be someone else and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say five, and I think seven names are mentioned. So you did see five out of the seven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, seven. I saw all of them that I said, five. However ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just ask you to look at those -- those paragraphs. So it's beginning -- beginning from 52 to 60. And just look at the names, review the names, 52 through 60. And can you -- can you tell us, again, whether -- after having reviewed the names, if there were any of those people that you did not see at the camp?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Rajko Kusic, Rajko Vukovic, I saw Mile Ujic. We were taken to a flat of Mile Ujic's and we cleaned it. He turned up, gave us some food. He was an officer and had some sort of insignia on him and they called him Captain. I can see one, two, three names here. Rajko, Jadranko, And Mile. Can I have a look at the others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next page for the witness, please. I think he has a hard copy of his statement, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further, Radomir Furtula. He would appear in the prison. Razdoljac, Djoko, yes. Carkic, Zoran, they said he was a security officer, captain for security. That's what the Serbs called him. And Stojan Perkovic, I saw him too. He was arrested and sentenced to 12 years in prison. The sentence was delivered in the court in Sarajevo. I know about Rajko Kusic for sure, and Radomir Furtula did appear in the prison. He conducted all the military operations around Rogatica and Gorazde. This was mentioned with Vinko, in a conversation with Vinko. I didn't hear this from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, moving onto a different topic. The -- I'd like to talk about the stipend that was mentioned from the Women Victims of War Organisation. Now, that stipend is from the -- actually from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina uses the Women Victims of War Organisation to distribute the money; is that correct? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I receive that money. As to where these funds come from, I have no idea. It's a non-governmental organisation, and we receive this sum every month.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to draw your attention now to the line of questions that you were asked about -- about your interaction with -- and again pardon my mispronunciation, with Hadzibulic's unit. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also remind you that your ten minutes are approximately over, so please wind up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Approximately over. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, you said at page 16, line 14, you were asked about automatic infantry weapons, and you responded: "I only saw such weapons on them." Can you tell us who "them" is?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 250 men who were to one side, and on the other side there were men without weapons. So they were Muslims. That's where I was lined up, and I saw those weapons on them. I didn't know them by name, but they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So that was approximately 250 of the 400 people that you described gathering there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were between 400 and 500 people. And that was that one half of them. I didn't count them. I didn't know whether there were 200 or 300 of them, but it was half of all those people whom I could not count.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Just two more questions, sir. Can you tell us those -- when you were there that day, the people that you saw there, did they appear otherwise organised? Did they have uniforms or other provisions that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any kind of uniform. They were summoned there on that day in order to organise themselves. There were no uniforms. They were all in civilian clothing. And there were no uniforms available of any kind in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you consider yourself to have been participating in any kind of organised armed resistance at any point from April of 1992 until 14 August 1992 when you were detained?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I didn't participate in anything. We gathered, one day we dug trenches, and there was this other day when we were doing road work. We hadn't been issued any orders, we were bored, and so we organised ourselves and spent two days working. And during that 20-day period I was taken captive, and as for what subsequently happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So it was a sum total of two days that you're -- you're talking about, interacting with Hadzibulic?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in contact with Hadzibulic around the 20th of July and only on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my re-direct. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions of the Prosecution triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. I do have to check with the client. He is trying to get my attention. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could Mr. Mladic speak at such a level of speech that others cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No -- no new questions raised by the re-direct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Hurko, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming and for answering all the questions that were put to you either by the parties or by the Bench. You're excused. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. For the next witness, no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then he can be called after we have resumed, and that will be at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are a couple of brief preliminary matters to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then before we -- yes. If you would please address them. We'll wait for the witness to be brought in, and -- please, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, before the witness is called in, I want to reiterate from our filing that Mr. Atlija's evidence does overlap in a limited way with adjudicated facts. We have reviewed Mr. Atlija's 92 ter material, and made certain redactions. We have also redacted certain paragraphs of Mr. Atlija's Croatian Information Centre statement, attached at Annex A, to his ICTY statement, now 65 ter 28368, in reliance on his ICTY statement at the Chamber's direction. I will suggest those paragraphs be unredacted if the Defence challenges the credibility of the relevant paragraphs of the ICTY statement. Regarding exhibits, I will refrain from tendering 26421 which was on our list, unless the relevant material in Mr. Atlija's 92 ter evidence is challenged. Regarding the other exhibits to be used with this witness, we have created and uploaded excerpts of two of the exhibits on our list. First, rather than showing the entire video bearing 65 ter 22594, we have created a 20-second clip from the video which has been assigned 65 ter number 22594A. Second, we have uploaded a version of 65 ter 26499, which includes only the cover page and the list of names about which the witness will directly testify. This has been assigned 65 ter 26499A. Is there any additional information the Chamber wishes me to provide at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. I see in the copy I have before me the 92 ter statement, I see that I have a numbered paragraph version, referring to adjudicated facts here and there. As far as the statement given to the Croatian Information Centre is concerned, and, of course, we were a bit surprised by it this morning, where are the redactions found? Oh, let me have a look at the other version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would give me a minute to just check the exhibit in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was uploaded fairly recently so it may have been printed out earlier. If you'd like, it might be useful for the Court Officer to call that exhibit to the screen. And that's 28368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Calling it to the screen now might not be of great assistance. I think since we often work both from hard copies and from the screen, if the Chamber would be provided by the redacted version of that statement in hard copy, then it's easier for us to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, and we'll get on to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then can the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And, meanwhile, I'll issue a decision on the -- oh, the witness is there already. I'll do it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Atlija, I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Atlija. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, you'll first be examined by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: My name is Ivo Atlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Atlija. Can you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I was born on the 19th of May, 1963, in the village of Brisevo, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I am a Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, do you remember providing a statement to the ICTY on 18 -- sorry, the 18th through the 20th of October, 2000?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28367 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Atlija, now that the document is on the screen before you, I'd ask you to view the first page; in particular, the signature in the bottom right-hand corner of the English version, and indicate whether you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can I ask that we go to page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, again, I'll ask you whether you recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, page 23, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, again, I'll ask you whether you recognise the signature on that page.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Atlija, in your statement, discussing grave number 1, including a group of about 20 Muslims in Stara Rijeka, the statement reflects that you think the grave was exhumed but you are not sure. Have you subsequently discovered what happened to the bodies of the people buried in this grave?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Through the media, I subsequently discovered that no bodies were found in that grave, but they were subsequently found in a grave called Jakarina Kosa, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in this statement discussing grave number 9, your statement reflects that the map attached at Annex B reflects the wrong location for grave number 9. Did you review Annex B to your statement, the map of grave-sites, in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And the grave is at the right location on the map that I had a look at, and this means that the error has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And on page 17 of your statement where you discuss grave number 13, your statement reflects that you are not sure if Mirsad Svraka's, I apologise for my mispronunciation, if that person's body has been exhumed. Have you since learned if the body has been exhumed?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Later I discovered through the press that the body had been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And now in annex A to your statement, 65 ter 28368, I just want to clear up two inconsistencies between the English and B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, if the Court Officer could pull up paragraph 20 of 65 ter 28368 on the third page each of the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, is the right number 200 Muslims or 2.000 Muslims that were killed in Redak?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The right number is about 200 Muslims. That's what I said, and that's what it says in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, second, if the Court Officer could pull up paragraph 24 on the fourth page of both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the B/C/S of this paragraph, it says that, and again I'll apologise for my pronunciation, Ivica Mlinar, Luka Mlinar, and Jerko Ivandic, were killed by pickaxes, shovels, and fence posts. In the English it say, Ivica Mlinar and Luka and Jerko Ivandic. Can you clarify for us whether Luka's last name was Mlinar or Ivandic?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Luka's last name is Mlinar. Ivandic is a mistake. There was only a Jerko Ivandic. So the last name was Mlinar. Ivica and Luka are Mlinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, have you had a chance to review your ICTY statement and its associated annexes in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I have had such a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And subject to the corrections we have just discussed, sir, if the Chamber takes your statement together with the annexes, will it have a correct picture of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there's nothing I would change.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if I were today to ask you questions about the material addressed therein, would you provide the same information, in substance?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide the same information for the simple reason that this information is truth and there is, therefore, no need to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28367, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28367 becomes Exhibit P168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P168 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours I would also, at this time tender the annexes to the statement as associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28368 becomes Exhibit P169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28369 becomes Exhibit P170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And document 28370 becomes Exhibit P171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there are two more annexes with 65 ter numbers 18458 and 18459.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18458 becomes Exhibit P172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And document 18459 becomes Exhibit P173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we now have those hard copies of the redacted version of what is now Exhibit P169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I meanwhile was informed that the only redaction is found on the second page. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There are substantial redactions on the second page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on the other pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As I recall, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the usher could assist. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now that the requirements of Rule 92 ter have been satisfied, I will briefly summarise Mr. Atlija's written evidence for the record. Ivo Atlija was born and raised in Prijedor municipality. In April 1992, he left Prijedor town after being sent home from his job on the orders of the SDS and returned to Brisevo, where his parents lived. From Brisevo, Mr. Atlija saw Serb forces attack Muslim villages in May of 1992. Hundreds of women and children came to Brisevo seeking refuge. They told him that the Serb army was burning their houses, killing men, and raping women. Mr. Atlija heard an ultimatum given to the Muslim village of Hambarine on behalf of the Prijedor Crisis Staff to surrender certain people or see the whole village burnt down. Then he saw soldiers and tanks enter the village. During the attack on Kozarac, he could see smoke rising and destroyed houses. On 27 May 1992, Brisevo was shelled. The next day, the villagers surrendered all their weapons. Check-points were set up around the village and men were taken away to detention camps. In the early morning of 24 July, Brisevo was attacked about large-calibre weapons. There was non-stop shelling. Regular soldiers and Chetniks burned down houses and looted them. All in all, 68 people were killed. Mr. Atlija was told that the 6th Krajina Brigade and the 5th Kozara Brigade were involved in the attack. The majority of the soldiers left during the course of 25 July. Mr. Atlija and other young men saw burned down houses and several buildings which had been damaged, including the Catholic church, and they helped bury the dead, starting with Mr. Atlija's own father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, now that I have summarised your written evidence, I'm going to ask several questions to clarify or expand upon that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask that the Court Officer call up 65 ter 13331 at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the area on this map?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the town of Prijedor in the map, and you can see the fish pound to the right in blue. And then there's a road towards Banja Luka to -- to the right. And that would be south-east, or to the east. And to the left, there is the read to Bosanski Novi. On the other side, to the south, there is the road for Ljubija. And above, if you follow this road from Prijedor to Ljubija, you pass through the village of Hambarine that has already been mentioned, and then you go a little further down in the direction of -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And did you have the chance to review this map in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, does it fairly and accurately depict the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite convinced that the map is a correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, is that a matter there's any dispute about it, or have you agreed with the -- is it challenged by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which matter exactly, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether this map accurately reflects the geographical situation. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We have not spoken to the Defence in that regard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it seems that unless there's any reason to believe that these kind of maps are inaccurate, that you could either agree with the Defence or leave it to cross-examination if there is any challenge to that, especially since you asked for additional time - which was not granted, by the way, yet, and we said we would see how examination-in-chief develops. And if you then start asking questions about whether the map is accurate or not, that, of course, might not be the best use of your time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this point I would request that 65 ter 13331 be admitted into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 13331 becomes Exhibit P174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And - let me just have a look - is this map also in the binder you tendered, Mr. Traldi? I just need to have a look at it. Because -- let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: On a quick review, Your Honour, I don't believe it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's a similar map. But, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's already assigned P174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for that. P174 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Atlija, after you left Prijedor you went to Brisevo. What was the atmosphere there like when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: At that time there was calm in Brisevo and the situation was relatively normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did that atmosphere change?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, in time it did change. The shooting was approaching. As time went by, Muslims came from the surrounding villages and told stories, and as I said the shooting approached both from Prijedor and from Sanski Most so that we were increasingly encircled. The situation was changing. The people were withdrawing, becoming withdrawn and afraid. And fear could be sensed. It was almost palpable. Because people felt helpless. They saw what was happening around them, and they were probably fearful that that would happen to us too, but nobody wanted to say it out loud. So the situation was becoming more and more hopeless and more and more bad for us. In addition, after a couple of weeks, the power supply was cut off, so we were unable anymore to watch television. The food in the refrigerators and freezers had gone bad. So people were becoming -- realising that it was turning for the worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would request that the Court Officer call 65 ter 18438 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the building in this picture?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This is the Brisevo Catholic church right before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd request that 65 ter 18438 be admitted into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18438 becomes Exhibit P175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask now that the Court Officer call up and play the video-clip bearing 65 ter number 22594A. I apologise, we'll be playing that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see now on the screen the interior of that same church that we had seen earlier. This is after the attack in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the same church but from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, at the end we saw the church tower. Do you know anything about what happened to the tower?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The church was destroyed and set on fire inside. And as for the tower, I believe it was demolished by, or, rather, destroyed by a hand-held launcher, a Zolja or some kind of anti-tank weapon. So the top of the tower was destroyed by this piece of weaponry, and -- as well as the bell tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd request that 65 ter 22594A be admitted into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video 22594A becomes Exhibit P176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, at paragraph 108 of Exhibit P168, your ICTY statement, in page 21 of the English and the B/C/S, you mention that all the Catholic churches and the mosque in Ljubija commune were destroyed. Can you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I'd just like to say that officially Ljubija was not a municipality at the time. The church and most of the other religious buildings were destroyed at that time during the attack. So the Brisevo church was destroyed in a direct attack on Brisevo. And as for the other religious buildings, they were destroyed within the next couple of weeks. Not all on one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, in your written evidence, you discuss victims named Mato Buzuk, Milan Buzuk, and others with the same last name. Did you ever learned what happened to someone named Morge Buzuk?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, I would also like to point out that Morge is not a name, it's actually a nickname. His last name was Buzuk and he worked at the same company where I worked and he was killed during the attack on Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will not go into further detail about the attack in reliance on adjudicated facts 919 through 924. I would, however, ask that the document marked 65 ter 26499A be called to our screens and that the Court Officer turn to page 3 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S original. And while that's coming up, Your Honours, this is one of the documents that I mentioned at the beginning. It's an excerpt from the list of persons from the Banja Luka bishopric killed during 1992 which was provided to OTP directly by the bishopric. Your Honour, as I -- apparently there is an issue with calling this exhibit up, I suggest that I move to the next area while it's called. Ah, now it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This is a list of people who were killed in the Brisevo area. But, for instance, the Matanovic family, they officially belonged to Stara Rijeka village, which was a border-line area between Brisevo and Stara Rijeka. Well, what's important to say is that this is a list of people who were killed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review this list during preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed it, and I think that I mentioned a number of names where I wasn't certain about the fate of those people. I didn't know them too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just to go over some of those brief names that you were not certain of sir. Looking at page 4 of the B/C/S, I understand you believed that the people listed at names 4 and 30 may have died elsewhere and not in Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And on page 5 of the B/C/S, I understand you do not know the people listed at names 55 and 66; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: 55 Ante Tokmacic [phoen], that's correct. I don't know the man. I can't recall him. As well as the name under 66, Tomislav Buleta. I'm not sure and I don't know what happened to that man. I don't know who that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The right name was not on the screen when you put the question to the witness. You should wait for the appearance of the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Especially if you only refer to numbers. There are so many numbers, starting from number 1 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: With regard to the remaining names, sir, you lived in Brisevo during the attack and participated in many of the burials of people who died during that attack. To the best of your knowledge, subject to the clarifications above, when did the remaining people listed here die?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Could you please clarify? I'm not sure I understood your question. Maybe I was a bit distracted. The people who were killed whose names appear on this list, they were all killed on the same day during the attack on Brisevo. Now, could you please repeat the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That -- that answers my question, actually, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 26499A as a public exhibit. And, for the record, I would note that it's the portion beginning at the title "Stara Rijeka" an ending just above the title "Surkovac" that we are suggesting that the witness can authenticate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that you referred to the names under Stara Rijeka. But when it was introduced, it was people being killed in Brisevo? Is that -- could we ask the witness whether that's the same, or is it where they were exhumed? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can clarify this. The title of the document says "Stara Rijeka," but I've just heard that this was obtained from the Banja Luka bishopric. Now, the village Presevo belonged to the bishopric of Stara Rijeka; however, most of these people were actually from Presevo and not from Stara Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that clarifies the matter. Mr. Traldi, you will only rely on the names mentioned under Stara Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? If not, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 26499A becomes Exhibit P177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P177 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, in your statements, you mention women who were raped. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber why you didn't want to give their names in your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, gladly. I did not want to give their names because those women were born, grew up, and lived in a very conservative Catholic environment, and any publication of their names would be additional suffering to them and they had suffered enough already. And, to the best of my abilities, I will never mention any of those names. If any of those women want to talk about it themselves, I don't object to that, but I will not be the one to disclose their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you see any of those women who had been raped subsequently?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I saw them and I talked with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what condition were they in at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Terrible condition. Suffice it to say that we had very much difficulty preventing some of them from committing suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Atlija, in your statements, for instance P168, paragraphs 105 to 107, you mention you were -- repeatedly spoke with Vojo Kupresanin about crimes that you said were committed by Serb forces? About how many times did you speak with Kupresanin in total?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I met with Vojo Kupresanin on three occasions, but we talked on the phone on many more occasions. I can't tell you exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in all those conversations, sir, did Kupresanin suggest, ever suggest, the possibility that anyone would be punished for the crimes you described to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, he never said a word about any of that. The only thing he did say was that he would try to intercede with General Talic so such things would stop. And he gave me access to the telephone service to Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did Kupresanin ever arrange a meeting for you with any other Serb leader?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Kupresanin organised a meeting with the then-mayor of the Serbian Prijedor municipality, Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you describe that meeting for us?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were three of us in the delegation. The meeting was relatively short. There was another man in Mr. Stakic's office together with Mr. Stakic. We later learned that his name was Sovanovic. I don't know exactly what his position was. I believe he was his deputy. They offered that they move us to intact houses that remained in the Muslim village of Biscani, but after a short conversation we declined that offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did Stakic or any other Serb leader you spoke with ever suggest the possibility that anyone would be punished for the crimes you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No. To this day, not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you spoke with Kupresanin and Stakic and other Serb leaders, what did you ask of them?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The only thing that I asked of them was to allow us to move out of that region without any impediments, and I will quote what I said then to Mr. Kupresanin in the presence of Mr. Rasula, who was the police commander in the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. There was also Bishop Komarica and some other people present. I said this to him: "Sir, you have territory, you've gained territory, so just allow people to move out from there. If you absolutely need to have Brisevo and those couple of hills there, you, the Serbian military, and the Serbian people, you can have them, but just let us go in peace." However, he did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in your meetings with Serb leaders and on the basis of those meetings, did you develop an impression why they were reluctant to let you leave?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, I can illustrate this. One of their excuses was, Listen, we have been accused of ethnic cleansing, and if we now let you go that will be an additional argument to accuse us of the same thing. And what I replied to that was, Well, what? And if you kill us all here, that wouldn't be ethnic cleansing? So I assumed they wanted to keep us there for some negotiations as hostages. Because Brisevo had no strategic significance in military terms or political or economic terms. And those couple of hills there, they were completely irrelevant. So it's a real shame that so many people died for nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Atlija, in Exhibit P168 you talk about how before the war, Brisevo was an almost completely Croatian village by ethnicity and it was destroyed. Not a single Croatian house left. Have any of the Croats who lived there subsequently returned?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No one returned to live there permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And have any of the homes been rebuilt?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, it would be more correct to say that three or four houses were built.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if no one has returned, sir, to live there, when are the houses used?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The only purpose of those houses is for us to meet there once a year to commemorate those unfortunate events. That is when a couple of hundred of people would gather there and we would use those homes so that we wouldn't have to stay out in the open, so that we would have a roof above our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. We had a few longer sessions this morning, therefore I think we should take a break now and then resume at 20 minutes to 2.00 for the remaining 25 minutes. Mr. Atlija, could you follow the usher. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I read out a decision. On the 30th of August, 2012, the Prosecution tendered the map book known under number 65 ter 28329. With the same limitations as with another map binder admitted already under P3, this map binder is now also admitted. I remind the parties of what the Chamber said in relation to P3, namely that, and I quote: "The Chamber recognises that the markings in P3 are mainly illustrations of the Prosecution's case which need to be proven by evidence. The Chamber aware of this and will not rely on these markings in making any findings. As a result, the map binder will be treated mainly as a reference." One second, please. Please be seated. This was the end of the quote. I add to that that P3 also continues photographs with descriptions. Although not technically markings, the Chamber will similarly not rely on such descriptions without other evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what I said is just valid both for the photographs in P3 and in 65 ter 28329, Madam Registrar, which will receive what exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28329 becomes Exhibit P178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is therefore admitted under this number with the same restrictions, as far as the use is concerned, as the Chamber decided for P3. Our apologies, Mr. Atlija, for letting you wait for a second. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to start of the cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Atlija, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Atlija.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we start?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you about certain events that took place in the immediate vicinity of the village of Brisevo. Do you know that on the 23rd of July, 1992, three Serbian soldiers were killed in the village of Raljas; Gojic, Milenko, Djuric, Borislav, and Curguz, Milan?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I heard that Milan Curguz was killed. As for whether it's in the village of Raljas, I don't know. But it was the wood called Borik where there was a certain path. But as to how he was killed and by whom, I do not know. I don't know about these other two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Gojic, Milenko, who was born in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The name is familiar, but I can't remember the face. But I did know Mr. Curguz.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear anything about who killed him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As far as Milan Curguz is concerned, there were several stories that I heard. One was that there was a quarrel between Serbian soldiers and that he was killed by a comrade-in-arms of his, a colleagues of his. The other story was that he was shot in a dispute with certain Muslims in the village of Kurevo. But as for what the truth is and what is no more than rumour, unfortunately, I'm not in a position to say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just waiting for the interpretation to finish. Did you hear that on the following day, Zoran Radulovic was killed? And this was also in the vicinity of the village of Raljas. This was on the 24th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I knew Zoran Radulovic personally. I heard that he had been killed, but as to how he was killed and by whom, I couldn't say. I also heard that he was killed somewhere in the vicinity of the Kurevo woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know or hear anything about Asim Muhic who led some of the armed men in the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Asim Muhic, no, I don't know him, but I know Aziz Aliskovic whose name appears in my statement, and you have certainly heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Aziz Aliskovic was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Asim Muhic was a lieutenant. But, very well, if you haven't heard of him. We'll return to the other issue of the people from Hambarine later on. Very briefly now, do you have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: If you mean my written statement, no, I don't have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we see Prosecution Exhibit ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It looks like I haven't noted down the number. It's a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be P168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see paragraph 3 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph -- in paragraph 3 you say: "I would also like to say that there is certain information in the statement that has to do with the military attack, and this was information provided to me by my friends."

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later you drew a map that showed the units that, according to you, participated in the attack on the village of Brisevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that is an amalgamation of the information you had, the information you obtained from conversations with other local inhabitants from your village; isn't that correct? Or is this information that you'd directly obtained -- it's not information that you directly obtained -- or not all of it is the information that you directly obtained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. I didn't directly obtain all the information. Some of the information was obtained from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And according to your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat his last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, could you please repeat your last question, Mr. Lukic. And, as I indicated already, to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Repeat the question for the sake of the transcript, not because you didn't answer my question: According to what you stated, you only saw one person being killed in the village of Brisevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your statement, you said that on that day 68 people were killed in the village of Brisevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at paragraph 9 in Mr. Atlija's statement. In this paragraph you say: "I was born in the village of Brisevo which is located in the local commune of Ljubija. The other villages that form part of the local commune were Ljubija, Zune, and Raljasi."

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to these villages that were part of Ljubija, were there other villages with a Croatian majority in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. There were Gornja Ravska, for example, Stara Rijeka. But Stara Rijeka was part of the Sanski Most municipality but it bordered on Brisevo. Gornja Ravska was also on the border with Brisevo, and these villages had a Croatian majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that these villages didn't suffer the same fate as Brisevo; that is to say, the Croats remained in those villages?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No. Not completely. The majority moved out as Stara Rijeka. As far as Gornja Ravska is concerned, I think that the majority remained in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Mr. Atlija, that many Croats in the municipality of Prijedor joined the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: When you say "many," a large number, I don't know what have you in mind. I know that about 100 or 105 people from the village of Gornja Ravska joined the army. It wasn't called the Army of Republika Srpska at the time. I don't know what the official name was, but they did join Serbian units. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now briefly move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, I would now like to take a look at paragraph 12 of your statement, where you talk about propaganda. Let us wait for it to come up on the screens. You don't have to read it. Can we agree that at this time all three sides engaged in propaganda?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I'm referring to propaganda that we had access to in Prijedor, that we were exposed to in Prijedor. I believe what you're saying, that all three sides, or all sides, were engaged in propaganda, but what I'm referring to here is the propaganda that we were exposed to in Prijedor municipality, and the propaganda that indoctrinated the citizens of Prijedor. And I'm talking about Prijedor because that is an area that I know things about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Isn't it correct that TV Zagreb could be watched, the programmes broadcast by TV Zagreb could be seen in Prijedor municipality because there were repeaters posted there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct. It is was possible to follow some programmes on Zagreb TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible or did you have reception of the broadcasts from TV Sarajevo because there was a repeater at Vlasic, Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, in Brisevo, as far as the time when I was there, it was not possible anymore to receive broadcasts from Sarajevo TV. Whether someone switched off the repeater at Mount Vlasic or not, I don't know, but we couldn't watch those programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before TV Sarajevo was switched off at Mrakovica, did you notice that TV Sarajevo stopped broadcasting programmes from Belgrade television?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, I know that the news at 7.30 or 8.00 p.m., the prime-time news, were broadcasts from different television centres, but that, too, stopped, but I couldn't tell you exactly at what time. I couldn't give you the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is sufficient to tell us what you know about. Thank you. You say then that the media were openly calling for all Serbs to take revenge and to pay back the old debts from the Second World War, newspapers started referring to Muslims and Croats as fundamentalists and Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that that had an effect on the local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, yes, it did have an impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you observe that, too, when armed Serbs came to your village of Brisevo, when they attacked it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: On that day, on the day of the attack itself, I was busy elsewhere, but immediately following this attack from conversations with others and when we had occasion to hear things they were talking about, I could say yes, it did have an impact on them, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also say that they kept repeating that Serbs, Orthodox Serbs, were threatened by fundamentalists and Ustashas who wanted to exterminate Serbs. Was it your impression that the Serbs believed this, that they really believed this?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, that's the sorry part. And to this day I really regret that they were actually certain that what they were thinking was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to refer you to paragraph 14 of your statement. In paragraph 14 you say the following: "The following couple of months I remained in Brisevo because it was impossible to go to Prijedor without a special permit that was issued by the Serb authorities in Ljubija."

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Serb civilians, too, had to obtain these permits to be allowed to move in Prijedor municipality? I'm talking about civilians.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: In the entire area of Prijedor municipality, I couldn't say with certainty. But I do know that people from Ljubija, people of Serb ethnicity from Ljubija, didn't have any difficulty travelling to Prijedor or moving about in Prijedor, or even travelling in their own vehicle, which, for us, was unthinkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, at the time, have occasion to move around, together with some Serb civilians at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, not together with a Serb civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, you don't know that they, too - in other words, the Serb civilians - had to have a permit in order to move around freely in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Now whether they had any permits or any kind of paper in their pockets, I really don't know anything about that, and I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who issued these permits, these passes, that allowed free movement; do you know?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, these permits were issued at the Serb so-called command. I don't know exactly the official name, but I know that it was run by the Taranjac brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could that have been a Crisis Staff in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is possible that this body was called a Crisis Staff, but in everyday speech we just referred to it as the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 16082 in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, when you testified, you said that these permits were issued by the Serbian Crisis Staff in Ljubija. Does this help refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible that that was called a Crisis Staff, but you will allow that after all these years, I may forget a detail or two -- I may have forgotten a detail or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who introduced the curfew in Prijedor municipality or in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Who and when the curfew was imposed in the entire Prijedor area, I don't know because I was probably already in Brisevo, and we were not very familiar with all the details in Prijedor as were the people who lived there, who lived in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now something of lesser importance, but you did mention it your statement in paragraph 15, and I know this is not of lesser significance to you, and my apologies, but you say in paragraph 15 that sometime in May of 1992, a Serb, by the name of Milan Mutic broke into my apartment and took up residence there and he still lives there. Of course, you gave this statement many years ago, so let me ask you whether in the meantime you were able to recover your property?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is correct, what you've said is correct. However, this man no longer lives in my apartment. And about four or five years ago - I'm not absolutely certain - through various international organisations and the current authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we managed to recover this property and to sell it, not to this man, not to Mutic, and not at the commercial, the ongoing market prices, but we did manage to sell it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now paragraphs 16 and 17 you say: "In early May 1992, several hundred Muslim women and children from those villages took shelter in Brisevo. They stayed in our village five or six days. Some of them later returned to their own village and others tried to get to Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Most of them were from Hambarine, and some left for Stari Majdan, Sanski Most, and others decided after a few days to return to Mataruska hills, as they referred to them. These are the hills where Muslim villages were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. We have to adjourn for the day. I first would like to instruct you, Mr. Atlija, that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is the testimony you gave today or whether testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is clear. Thank you, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom. And you now may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 6th of September, 9.30 a.m. in this same courtroom, I.
